questions.question_text: Which of the following is a good prognostic factor for dissociative amnesia?

options.text: Sudden onset with a clearly identifiable precipitant

correct_answer.text: Sudden onset with a clearly identifiable precipitant

questions.explanation: Good prognostic factors for dissociative amnesia include sudden onset, brief duration, presence of a clearly identifiable acute precipitant, absence of comorbid psychiatric disorders, and good premorbid functioning. Prolonged or recurrent/intermittent episodes (Option A) are poor prognostic indicators. Comorbid depersonalization (Option C) and early onset (Option D) are also associated with poorer outcomes.

questions.question_text: A wife brings her husband to the emergency room (ER) presenting with unusual behavior. She noted that he doesn’t remember her or his name, his job, and is acting like a child. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation: This case presents a classic description of dissociative amenia, including a patient with a history of an acute trauma and physical symptoms including alterations in consciousness, a trance state, age regression, anterograde dissociative amnesia, etc.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which is not a predisposing factor for the development of peptic ulcer?
questions.explanation: Lifestyle factors predict the development of peptic ulcer in susceptible individuals. They are potential mediators in the aetiological matrix between stress and ulcer. These include cigarette smoking; heavy alcohol consumption; lack of sleep; not eating breakfast; non-steroidal anti-infl ammatory drugs; hard on-the-job labour and low socioeconomic status. Lloyd G and Guthrie E. Handbook of Liaison Psychiatry, illustrated edition. Cambridge University Press, 2007. p. 392.

questions.question_text: A female patient presents to A&E with sudden aphonia following her mother coming to live with her. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation: Sudden loss of voice (aphonia) following a specific stressor without organic pathology is characteristic of motor dissociative disorder.

questions.question_text: A woman presents with multiple gynecological and gastric complaints over 10 years with all tests normal. She is convinced doctors have missed something. Which diagnosis is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Bodily distress disorder (formerly somatization) is characterized by persistent bodily symptoms with excessive attention directed toward them, excessive health-related behaviors, and symptoms not alleviated by appropriate clinical examination and reassurance, lasting for at least several months.

questions.question_text: Exaggerated and catastrophic misinterpretation of body signs and symptoms is characteristic of which condition?
questions.explanation: Hypochondriasis is characterized by exaggerated and catastrophic misinterpretation of body signs and symptoms.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old woman with asthma becomes extremely anxious when she gets an upper respiratory infection. She presents to the emergency department with complaints of being unable to breathe. While there, she begins to hyperventilate and then reports feeling extremely dizzy. Her hyperventilation causes her to become fatigued, and when the medical evaluation indicates that she is retaining carbon dioxide (CO ), it becomes necessary to admit her. The woman 2 denies any other symptoms beyond anxiety. What is the most suitable diagnosis?

options.text: A diagnosis of acute stress disorder.
A diagnosis of generalized anxiety disorder.
A diagnosis of adjustment disorder with anxiety.
Psychological factors affecting other medical conditions.

correct_answer.text: Psychological factors affecting other medical conditions.

questions.explanation: In psychological factors affecting other medical conditions, specific psychological entities (e.g., psychological symptoms, behaviors, other factors) exacerbate a medical condition. These psychological factors can precipitate, exacerbate, or put an individual at risk for medical illness, or they can worsen an existing condition. In contrast, an adjustment disorder is a reaction to the stressor (e.g., having a medical illness).

questions.question_text: A man witnessed his friend's death 6 weeks ago and is now unable to move a limb despite the absence of any neurological deficit. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Conversion disorder (Dissociative neurological symptom disorder in ICD-11)

correct_answer.text: Conversion disorder (Dissociative neurological symptom disorder in ICD-11)

questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of physical symptoms (limb paralysis) without neurological explanation following a psychologically traumatic event is consistent with conversion disorder, now called Dissociative neurological symptom disorder in ICD-11.

questions.question_text: Which of the following DSM-5 criteria are no longer required for a diagnosis of a somatic disorder?

options.text: Persistent belief of an undetected disease
Symptoms that cannot be medically explained

correct_answer.text: Symptoms that cannot be medically explained

questions.explanation: An older perspective for somatic disorders involved only including symptoms that could not be medically explained. We now know that patients with medically established diagnoses can have a disproportionate amount of anxiety or physical symptoms from their medical disorder. Thus, in DSM-5, it is no longer required for symptoms to be medically unexplained.

questions.question_text: Over a period of several years, a 50-year-old woman visits her dermatologist’s office every few weeks to be evaluated for skin cancer, showing the dermatologist various freckles, nevi, and patches of dry skin about which she has become concerned. None of the skin findings have ever been abnormal, and the dermatologist has repeatedly reassured her. The woman does not have pain, itching, bleeding, or other somatic symptoms. She does have a prior diagnosis of occasional panic attacks. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: A diagnosis of unspecified anxiety disorder.
A diagnosis of illness anxiety disorder.
A diagnosis of somatic symptom disorder.

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of illness anxiety disorder.

questions.explanation: One should consider the possibility that the presenting problem is better accounted for by another psychiatric disorder that would preclude a diagnosis of illness anxiety disorder, but the mere presence of another anxiety symptom (panic attacks) is not sufficient to conclude that another anxiety disorder diagnosis better explains the patient’s problem. Illness anxiety disorder is the appropriate diagnosis because the patient has no somatic symptom but does have a persistent worry that she has a serious illness (skin cancer), is easily alarmed by minor somatic changes (patches of dry skin), and repeatedly and excessively seeks reassurance through medical checkups, with persistence of the problem for more than 6 months. The term hypochondriasis as a synonym for illness anxiety is no longer used as a diagnostic label. The absence of a somatic symptom rules out somatic symptom disorder. Factitious disorder entails willful falsification of signs or symptoms.

questions.question_text: After finding a breast lump, a 53-year-old woman with a family prior diagnosis of breast cancer is overwhelmed by feelings of anxiety. Consultation with a breast surgeon, mammogram, and biopsy show the lump to be benign. The surgeon indicates that she requires no treatment; however, she continues to ruminate about the possibility of cancer and surgery that will result in disfigurement. Her sleep is restless and she is having trouble concentrating at work. After 6weeks in this state, her primary physician requests that she consult a psychiatrist. On initial evaluation the patient weeps throughout the interview, and is so distraught that the evaluator is unable to elicit details of her medical and psychiatric history beyond reviewing the current “crisis.” Which diagnosis most accurately describes this clinical presentation?
questions.explanation:
The patient is experiencing marked distress and functional impairment (trouble concentrating at work, extreme weeping) that is entirely focused on a specific, identifiable psychosocial stressor (finding a breast lump). Her reaction is out of proportion to the current severity of the stressor, given that the lump has been definitively diagnosed as benign. Because her symptoms developed within 3 months of the stressor and do not meet the criteria for another specific psychiatric disorder, Adjustment Disorder is the most accurate diagnosis.

Illness anxiety disorder involves a preoccupation with having or acquiring a serious illness, but DSM-5 diagnostic criteria require this preoccupation to be present for at least 6 months. This patient\'s symptoms have only been present for 6 weeks.

Acute stress disorder requires exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence, and symptoms must resolve within 1 month of the traumatic event. A benign breast lump biopsy does not meet the trauma criterion, and her symptoms have persisted beyond the 1-month threshold.

Generalized anxiety disorder requires excessive, difficult-to-control worry about multiple different events or activities (rather than a single stressor) occurring more days than not for at least 6 months.

Major depressive disorder requires at least five specific depressive symptoms (such as pervasive depressed mood, anhedonia, suicidality, or weight changes) present for at least two weeks. While she has sleep and concentration difficulties, her clinical picture is dominated by stress-induced anxiety and rumination rather than a pervasive major depressive episode.

questions.question_text: Which feature best distinguishes transient global amnesia from dissociative amnesia?

options.text: Transient global amnesia occurs in association with cerebrovascular disease.
Both resolve quickly over a few hours without residual cognitive symptoms.
Stressful life events can precede either of them.
Loss of personal identity occurs in transient global amnesia but not in dissociative amnesia.

correct_answer.text: Transient global amnesia occurs in association with cerebrovascular disease.

questions.explanation: Transient global amnesia is an organic syndrome, typically in older patients with vascular risk factors, attributed to transient hypoperfusion/ischaemia or venous congestion in medial temporal (limbic–hippocampal) structures; it presents with abrupt, dense anterograde amnesia with variable retrograde amnesia, preserved personal identity, and resolution within 24 hours (SPMM Paper B p.393; Shorter Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry 8e p.335). Dissociative amnesia, by contrast, is psychogenic, characteristically retrograde and autobiographical, with loss of personal identity in the fugue subtype, and may persist for days or longer (SPMM Paper A p.67; DSM-5-TR p.501). Hence option A captures the key organic/cerebrovascular distinction. B is false because dissociative amnesia does not reliably remit within hours; C inverts the anterograde/retrograde pattern; D describes a shared precipitant rather than a difference; E names an unrelated diagnostic entity.

questions.question_text: What is the essential diagnostic feature of factitious disorder?
questions.explanation: The essential feature of factitious disorder is the falsification of medical or psychological signs and symptoms in oneself or others that are associated with identified deception in the absence of obvious external rewards.

questions.question_text: Somatisation disorder is now termed which diagnosis in ICD-11?
questions.explanation: Somatisation disorder is now classified as bodily distress disorder in ICD-11, characterized by preoccupation with multiple bodily symptoms affecting multiple body systems.

questions.question_text: A person experiences a loss of awareness of their own body and feels disconnected from it. What is this dissociative symptom called?
questions.explanation: Depersonalization is the loss of awareness of one's own body and feeling detached or disconnected from one's physical self, as if observing the body from outside.

questions.question_text: After an airplane flight, a 60-year-old woman with a prior diagnosis of chronic anxiety develops deep vein thrombophlebitis and a subsequent pulmonary embolism. Over the next year, she focuses relentlessly on sensations of pleuritic chest pain and repeatedly seeks medical attention for this symptom, which she worries is due to recurrent pulmonary emboli, despite negative test results. Review of systems reveals that she also has chronic back pain and that she has consulted many physicians for symptoms of culture-negative cystitis. What diagnosis most accurately describes this clinical picture?

options.text: A diagnosis of post–pulmonary embolism syndrome.
A diagnosis of chest pain syndrome.
A diagnosis of somatic symptom disorder.

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of somatic symptom disorder.

questions.explanation: This patient's pain preoccupations, anxiety about her symptoms, and medical care–seeking behaviors in the aftermath of her pulmonary embolism are the basis for making the diagnosis of somatic symptom disorder. The issue of whether her pleuritic pain symptoms can be explained as caused by her previous pulmonary embolism is not relevant to this determination; what matters is her abnormal appraisal of, focus on, and behavioral response to the pain. In the DSM-IV classification, she might have received a dual diagnosis of hypochondriasis and pain disorder; in DSM-5 her anxiety about the significance of her somatic symptoms and her ongoing pain complaints point to a diagnosis of somatic symptom disorder.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which statements about the psychodynamic origins of adjustment disorder is Accurate?

options.text: Early childhood trauma may predispose to adjustment disorder later in life.
Children who identify with their mother more than their father are at higher risk of developing adjustment disorder.
Psychological predisposition to adjustment disorder is independent of the stage of the life cycle.
Prior to development of the superego, every child has equal vulnerability to stress.
Early childhood trauma increases resilience in adulthood.

correct_answer.text: Early childhood trauma may predispose to adjustment disorder later in life.

questions.explanation: Children who suffer more earlylife trauma tend to develop less mature defense mechanisms. In later life these individuals may have greater difficulty coping with stressors, thus predisposing to adjustment disorder.

questions.question_text: A 24yearold student from Bogotá, Colombia, starts college in the United States. After 1 month, the student’s adviser is concerned that she may be depressed. Although the student speaks English well, she does not know anyone in town. Her family is in Bogotá, and she does not anticipate seeing them soon. She has not made many friends. She is not able to concentrate in her classes and is easily irritated. She denies poor sleep, poor appetite, loss of interest in hobbies, feelings of guilt, decreased energy, or suicidal ideation. Which of the following is the MOST likely diagnosis?

options.text: A diagnosis of major depressive disorder
A diagnosis of schizotypal personality disorder
A diagnosis of schizoid personality disorder

questions.explanation: According to DSM5, adjustment disorder is the development of emotional or behavioral symptoms in response to an identifiable stressor or stressors occurring within 3 months of the onset of the stressor. It is characterized by marked distress that is out of proportion to the severity or intensity of the stressor, taking into account the external context and the cultural factors that might influence symptom severity and presentation. It is associated with significant impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which diagnostic requirements differentiates malingering from factitious disorder, somatic symptom disorder, illness anxiety disorder, and conversion disorder?

options.text: The individual seeks to be a individual and experience the sick role.
Malingering involves the presence of an external incentive.

correct_answer.text: Malingering involves the presence of an external incentive.

questions.explanation: In malingering, there is an external incentive (e.g., avoiding work or obtaining money), whereas factitious disorder has no other incentive than to be a patient and experience the 228 • PSYCHIATRY sick role. In malingering and factitious disorder, patients provide false information and behave deceptively, but in somatic symptom disorder, illness anxiety disorder, and conversion disorder, there is no evidence that patients are deceiving clinicians. Re FeRe NCe American Psychiatric Association. (2013). Diagnostic and statistical manual of mental disorders (5th ed.). Arlington, VA: American Psychiatric Publishing. Bass, C., & Halligan, P. (2014). questions.question_text: A 20-year-old man presents with acute onset of decreased visual acuity in his left eye. Physical, neurological, and laboratory examinations (including brain MRI) are entirely normal. The patient also reports that since his midteens he has felt his left cheekbone and eyebrow are too big, spending a lot of time comparing sides of his face in the mirror, and plans to have plastic surgery. Which pair of diagnoses is most appropriate?

options.text: Body dysmorphic disorder and conversion disorder
Delusional disorder and somatic symptom disorder
Illness anxiety disorder and body dysmorphic disorder
Somatic symptom disorder and conversion disorder
Somatic symptom disorder and illness anxiety disorder

correct_answer.text: Body dysmorphic disorder and conversion disorder

questions.explanation: The vision complaint and normal examinations are consistent with a diagnosis of a functional neurological symptom disorder (conversion disorder). The long-standing concern about the appearance of the left side of his face is consistent with a diagnosis of body dysmorphic disorder. An individual can have both of these diagnoses.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about depersonalization/derealization disorder is TRUE regarding its epidemiology and gender distribution? (Note: The original stem was truncated. Based on the explanation, the intended question concerned gender prevalence — specifically that women and men are equally affected, with a 1:1 ratio, mean age of onset of 16 years, and only 5% of cases beginning after age 25.)

options.text: It affects women significantly more often than men.
It affects women and men with equal frequency (1:1 ratio).
The mean age of onset is typically after age 25.
Transient symptoms of the disorder are extremely rare in the general population.
Onset of the disorder commonly occurs after age 40

correct_answer.text: It affects women and men with equal frequency (1:1 ratio).

questions.explanation: Depersonalization/derealization disorder affects women and men with equal frequency, giving a gender ratio of 1:1. The mean age of onset is 16 years, with less than 20% experiencing onset after age 20 and only 5% after age 25 — onset after age 40 is highly unusual. Transient depersonalization/derealization symptoms are common in the general population (approximately half of all adults experience at least one lifetime episode), but symptomatology meeting full diagnostic criteria is markedly less common, with a one-month prevalence in the UK of approximately 1–2%.

questions.question_text: Hypochondriasis is currently classified in the DSM-5 under which category?
questions.explanation: Hypochondriasis is classified under OCD and Related Disorders in ICD-11, characterized by abnormal preoccupation with one's health and fear of disease despite physical evidence to the contrary.

questions.question_text: Which personality disorder is most commonly comorbid with dissociative identity disorder?

options.text: A diagnosis of borderline personality disorder
A diagnosis of paranoid personality disorder
A diagnosis of dependent personality disorder
A diagnosis of avoidant personality disorder
A diagnosis of obsessive-compulsive personality disorder

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of borderline personality disorder

questions.explanation: Dissociative identity disorder (DID) is most commonly comorbid with borderline personality disorder (BPD). The DSM-5-TR notes that individuals with DID \'often present identities that appear to encapsulate a variety of severe personality disorder features,\' and BPD is the most frequently documented comorbid personality disorder in clinical studies of DID, sharing features such as emotional dysregulation, identity disturbance, and a history of trauma. Paranoid personality disorder is not specifically linked to DID. Dependent and avoidant personality disorders, while sometimes present, are not the primary personality disorder association with DID.

questions.question_text: A 39yearold female patient is brought to a neurologist by her partner with complaints of episodic difficulty speaking. She says that during these episodes her voice has a “strangled” sound to it but then resolves spontaneously. She describes also seeing “sharp kitchen knives” in her vision when she develops this dysphonia. Further evaluation reveals a history of childhood abuse. Brain MRI during one of these episodes reveals no significant abnormalities. Which of the following diagnoses is most likely?

options.text: A diagnosis of somatic symptom disorder
A diagnosis of illness anxiety disorder

questions.explanation: According to the US Department of Education, in 2012– 2013 children received special education most commonly for a specific learning disability such as in math, reading, or writing. Specific learning disability was the cause for 35% of patients in special education. Autism accounted for 8%, intellectual disability accounted for 7%, emotional disturbance accounted for 6%, and ADHD under the classification of “other health impairment” accounted for 12% of patients in special education.

questions.question_text: Dissociative disorders involve disruptions or discontinuities in the operation and integration of many areas of psychological functioning. which of the following options is not a functional area affected in dissociative disorders?
questions.explanation: Dissociative disorders encompass disruptions and discontinuities in many areas of psychological functioning, including normal integration of consciousness, memory, identity, emotion, perception, body representation, motor control, and behavior. If frank psychotic symptoms such as delusional beliefs are present, one must consider a diagnosis outside the dissociative disorders arena to account for the symptoms.

questions.explanation: Recurrent headaches are the most common somatic symptom with no medical explanation complained by children, followed by abdominal pain. 10 to 30% of children admit having frequent headaches (at least weekly) while 7 to 25% admit having abdominal pain. Chest pain is reported by approximately 10% of school aged children. At least 7.5% of children admit to other musculoskeletal pains. questions.question_text: Ganser syndrome is classified as which type of disorder?
questions.explanation: Ganser syndrome is classified as a dissociative disorder, characterized by approximate answers and other dissociative features.

questions.question_text: A 60-year-old man has prostate cancer with bony metastases that cause persistent pain. He is treated with antiandrogen medications that result in hot flashes. He is unable to work because of his symptoms, but he is stoical, hopeful, and not anxious. What is the appropriate diagnosis?

options.text: A diagnosis of illness anxiety disorder.
A diagnosis of somatic symptom disorder.
The man's pain is likely secondary to psychological factors rather than cancer.

questions.explanation: This patient has “medically explained” symptoms, but they are still somatic symptoms that result in disruption of important daily life functions. He therefore meets Criterion A for somatic symptom disorder; however, he does not meet Criterion B, which requires excessive thoughts, feelings, or behaviors related to the symptoms. Pain disorder is not a DSM-5 diagnostic category. The patient has a somatic symptom but is not anxious, so he does not have illness anxiety disorder. The diagnosis psychological factors affecting other medical conditions refers to emotional, cognitive, or behavioral issues that worsen prognosis or interfere with management of a physical condition; that diagnosis would not apply to the patient in this vignette.

questions.question_text: Which of the following DSM-5 criteria for depersonalization/derealization disorder is only present for derealization symptoms and not for depersonalization?
questions.explanation: While feelings that things aren’t real can be a part of depersonalization or derealization symptoms, the only other DSM-5 criteria to describe derealization includes feeling detached from one’s surroundings. Depersonalization symptoms including feeling detached from oneself and feeling as if observing oneself, along with time and perceptual distortions.

questions.question_text: Ganser syndrome is classified under which diagnostic category?
questions.explanation: Ganser syndrome is classified as a dissociative disorder, characterized by approximate answers and dissociative features.

options.text: individuals unconsciously amplify normal physiological function.

individuals often have high autonomic arousal.

questions.explanation: Primary somatic symptom disorders may be associated with a heightened awareness of normal bodily sensations. This heightened awareness may be paired with a cognitive bias to interpret any physical symptom as indicative of medical illness. Autonomic arousal may be high in some patients with somatization. Imaging studies support an association between one or more of the somatic symptom disorders with reduced volume of the brain amygdala and brain connectivity between the amygdala and brain regions controlling executive and motor function. questions.question_text: A patient has visited 5 hospitals and all tests are normal, but he is not accepting this and is convinced he has cancer. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This describes delusional disorder (somatic type), where the patient maintains a fixed false belief (cancer) despite objective evidence to the contrary, showing poor insight.

questions.question_text: A patient who believes he has cancer despite negative Frequent clinical findings and appropriate medical evaluation most likely has:
questions.explanation: Illness anxiety disorder (DSM-5; formerly hypochondriasis in DSM-IV) is characterised by preoccupation with having or acquiring a serious illness despite negative or minimal somatic findings and appropriate medical reassurance, as described in DSM-5-TR (F45.21). Somatic symptom disorder involves excessive distress about actual somatic symptoms rather than disease conviction alone. Conversion disorder presents with motor or sensory deficits that suggest neurological disease but are caused by psychological factors. Factitious disorder involves the voluntary, conscious production of symptoms to assume the sick role, distinguishing it from illness anxiety disorder where there is no deliberate feigning.

questions.question_text: Regarding non-epileptic seizures, which statement is TRUE?

options.text: 1 in 10 patients referred to specialized epilepsy services have non-epileptic seizures
9 in 10 patients with non-epileptic seizures are women
Epilepsy cannot coexist with non-epileptic seizures
Non-epileptic seizures always develop after epilepsy

correct_answer.text: 9 in 10 patients with non-epileptic seizures are women

questions.explanation: Approximately 9 in 10 patients presenting with non-epileptic seizures are female; they are more common in women and may coexist with genuine epilepsy.

questions.question_text: A female patient presents with multiple gynecological and gastrointestinal symptoms. Multiple doctors have been consulted with no organic pathology identified. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation: Somatization disorder (now called bodily distress disorder in ICD-11) is characterized by multiple somatic symptoms across different body systems that cause significant distress and impair functioning, with medical evaluation typically failing to identify adequate organic pathology.

questions.question_text: Criterion B for the diagnosis of dissociative identity disorder (DID) requires recurrent gaps in the recall of everyday events, important personal information, and/or traumatic events that are inconsistent with ordinary forgetting. which of the following options statements about Criterion B–qualifying amnesia is inaccurate?

options.text: Gaps in recall of remote life events do not meet Criterion B definitions for amnesia.
It is common for patients with DID to minimize their amnesia symptoms.

Patients with DID may discover evidence of their past actions or experiences, such as finding clothing in the closet they do not recall buying, or seeing a photo of a trip they don’t recall taking. Dissociative Disorders—QUESTIONS | 71
Amnesia for procedural skills like driving is not considered Criterion B amnesia.
Dissociative fugues in which an patients finds him- or herself in a location with no memory of having traveled there are common in DID and represent a form of amnesia.

correct_answer.text: Gaps in recall of remote life events do not meet Criterion B definitions for amnesia.

questions.explanation: The dissociative amnesia of individuals with DID manifests in three primary ways: as 1) gaps in remote memory of personal life events (e.g., periods of childhood or adolescence; some important life events, such as the death of a grandparent, getting married, giving birth); 2) lapses in dependable memory (e.g., of what happened today, of well-learned skills such as how to do their job, use a computer, read, drive); and 3) discovery of evidence of their everyday actions and tasks that they do not recollect doing (e.g., finding unexplained objects in their shopping bags or among their possessions; finding perplexing writings or drawings that they must have created; discovering injuries; “coming to” in the midst of doing something). Dissociative fugues, wherein the person discovers dissociated travel, are common. Thus, individuals with DID may report that they have suddenly found themselves at the beach, at work, in a nightclub, or somewhere at home (e.g., in the closet, on a bed or sofa, in the corner) with no memory of how they came to be there. Amnesia in individuals with DID is not limited to stressful or traumatic events; these individuals often cannot recall everyday events as well.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which is the BEST established treatment modality for somatic symptom and related disorders?
questions.explanation: CBT is the best established treatment modality for somatic symptom and related disorders.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which is not considered a feature of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS)?

options.text: Abdominal discomfort not relieved by defaecation

correct_answer.text: Abdominal discomfort not relieved by defaecation

questions.explanation: IBS is the prototypical functional gastrointestinal disorder characterized by abdominal pain and diarrhoea or constipation. The International Congress of Gastroenterology has developed a standardized set of criteria for IBS. They include either abdominal pain relieved by defaecation or associated with a change in frequency or consistency of stool; or disturbed defaecation involving two or more of the following: altered stool frequency; altered stool form hard or loose and watery; altered stool passage straining or urgency or feeling of incomplete evacuation; passage of mucus. IBS can be categorized into diarrhoea-predominant, constipation-predominant, and mixed subtypes. Medical treatment often targets the predominant symptom. IBS accounts for as much as 50% of all outpatient evaluations done by gastroenterologists. Kaplan HI. Kaplan and Sadock’s Comprehensive Textbook of Psychiatry, 8th edn. Lippincott Williams and Wilkins, 2004 p. 2115.

questions.explanation: All of these are examples of behaviors seen in adjustment disorder with disturbance of conduct.

questions.question_text: A man whose friend died in a motorcycle accident now has a paralyzed arm despite no neurological abnormality on examination. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation: Conversion disorder (now called functional neurological symptom disorder) presents with neurological symptoms without organic pathology, often related to psychological stressors.

questions.question_text: In which of the following conditions are both the mechanism of illness production and the motivation for illness behavior conscious?

options.text: A diagnosis of somatic symptom disorder
A diagnosis of illness anxiety disorder

questions.explanation: Contrary to the DSM-I V-T R somatoform disorders, somatic symptom disorder and illness anxiety disorder focus on the presence of distress rather than the absence of medical cause. That is, they are not conceptualized as “psychogenic” conditions as was somatization disorder. Nevertheless, somaticizing (translation of psychological distress into somatic complaints) and somatosensory amplification (amplification of somatic symptoms by psychological distress) play a significant role in many, though not all, instances of somatic symptom disorder. In conversion, both the mechanism of illness production (MIP) and the motivation for illness behavior (MIB) are unconscious. In malingering, both MIP and MIB are conscious in that the patient knows what he or she is doing and why (secondary gain). Factitious disorder is characterized by conscious MIP but unconscious MIB. Re FeRe NCe Yates, W. R. (2014) Somatic symptom disorders clinical presentation. Retrieved from http:// emedicine.medscape.com/ article/ 294908clinical

Her sleep, appetite, and energy are normal, and she denies suicidal thoughts. She reports a recent stressor, namely, breaking up with her boyfriend 1 week before the end of the semester. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?

options.text: A diagnosis of major depressive disorder
A diagnosis of generalized anxiety disorder

questions.explanation: The patient’s presentation is most consistent with adjustment disorder with depressed mood. Adjustment disorder is the development of emotional or behavioral symptoms in response to an identifiable stressor that occurs within 3 months of the onset of the stressor and lasts no longer than 6 months after the stressor or its consequences have ceased.

Psychological factors affecting other medical conditions

correct_answer.text: Psychological factors affecting other medical conditions

questions.explanation: According to DSM5, psychological factors affecting other medical conditions are seen when a medical symptom or condition is present and is characterized by psychological or behavioral factors that adversely affect the medical condition in one of the following ways: Factors have influenced the course of the medical condition as shown by a close temporal association between the psychological factors and the development or exacerbation of, or delayed recovery from, the medical condition; factors interfere with the treatment of the medical condition; factors constitute additional wellestablished health risks for the individual; and factors influence the underlying pathophysiology, precipitating or exacerbating symptoms or necessitating medical attention. questions.question_text: A woman with 10 years of multiple gynecological and gastric pain complaints with all tests normal and conviction that doctors missed something most likely has
questions.explanation: This presentation is consistent with bodily distress disorder (ICD-11), characterized by persistent distressing bodily symptoms with excessive health-related behaviors despite normal investigations; bodily distress focuses on symptoms whereas hypochondriasis focuses on illness fear.

questions.question_text: A motorcyclist paralyzed in one limb following an accident with no apparent neurological basis is most likely diagnosed with:
questions.explanation: Conversion disorder (now called Dissociative Neurological Symptom Disorder in ICD-11) presents with neurological symptoms such as paralysis without identified neurological pathology following a psychologically stressful event.

questions.question_text: Criterion A for the diagnosis of dissociative identity disorder (DID) requires the presence of two or more distinct personality states or an experience of possession. which of the following options symptom presentations would not qualify as a manifestation of an alternate identity?

options.text: An intrusive voice would qualify as Criterion A only if heard multiple times daily.
Sudden mood changes not attributed to stressors would qualify as identity change.
Shifts in personality preferences about clothing would qualify as identity alteration.
Feeling temporarily disoriented about age or body would meet Criterion A requirements.
A religious experience of being reborn into a new spiritual state that affects multiple domains of the patients’s behavior.

correct_answer.text: A religious experience of being reborn into a new spiritual state that affects multiple domains of the patients’s behavior.

questions.explanation: Personality changes do not qualify as part of Criterion A symptoms if they are a normal part of a broadly accepted cultural or religious practice. Personality changes that do count toward Criterion A are related to discontinuities of experience that can affect any aspect of an individual’s functioning. Individuals with dissociative identity disorder may report the feeling that they have suddenly become depersonalized observers of their “own” speech and actions, which they may feel powerless to stop (sense of self). Such individuals may also report perceptions of voices (e.g., a child’s voice; crying; the voice of a spiritual being). In some cases, voices are experienced as multiple, perplexing, independent thought streams over which the individual experiences no control. Strong emotions, impulses, and even speech or other actions may suddenly emerge, without a sense of personal ownership or control (sense of agency). These emotions and impulses are frequently reported as ego-dystonic and puzzling. Attitudes, outlooks, and personal preferences (e.g., about food, activities, dress) may suddenly shift and then shift back. Individuals may report that their bodies feel different (e.g., like a small child, like the opposite gender, huge and muscular). Alterations in sense of self and loss of personal agency may be accompanied by a feeling that these attitudes, emotions, and behaviors—even one’s body—are “not mine” and/or are “not under my control.”

questions.question_text: Which dissociative disorder involves inability to remember personal identity?
questions.explanation: Dissociative identity disorder involves inability to recall personal identity and the presence of distinct personality states.

questions.question_text: A 19-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his family with acute onset of hemoptysis. Although he denies any role in the genesis of the symptom, he is observed in the waiting area to be surreptitiously inhaling a solution that provokes violent coughing. On confrontation he eventually acknowledges his action but explains that he heard an angel’s voice instructing him to purify himself for a divine mission for which he will receive a heavenly reward. He was therefore trying to expunge all “evil vapors” from his lungs but felt obliged to keep this a secret. Why would this patient not be considered to have factitious disorder? Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders—QUESTIONS | 77

options.text: The presentation suggests malingering rather than factitious disorder.
Factitious disorder cannot be diagnosed in patients under age 21.
The symptoms are too obvious to represent true factitious disorder.
Factitious disorder requires a documented history of multiple hospital admissions.
The presence of a psychotic illness that better accounts for the symptoms precludes the diagnosis of factitious disorder.

correct_answer.text: The presence of a psychotic illness that better accounts for the symptoms precludes the diagnosis of factitious disorder.

questions.explanation: The presence of bizarre delusions and command auditory hallucinations strongly suggests a psychotic disorder. When another mental illness better accounts for the presentation, a diagnosis of factitious disorder should not be made (Criterion D). DSM-5 seeks to be respectful of variations in experience and modes of self-expression that are aspects of an individual’s cultural and religious background, but it is unlikely that such factors would result in fabrication of illness presentation, and “rewards from heaven” would not generally be considered to be “obvious external rewards.” Factitious disorder is more common in women, but it also occurs in men. Both single and recurrent episodes of fabrication qualify for diagnosis and should be specified.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old woman is unable to remember a traumatic experience. Which dissociative disorder best describes her presentation?
questions.explanation: Dissociative amnesia is characterized by the inability to recall important autobiographical information, typically related to a traumatic or stressful event, which matches this patient's presentation of being unable to remember a traumatic experience.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which symptoms is incompatible with a diagnosis of conversion disorder (functional neurological symptom disorder)? Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders—QUESTIONS | 75

options.text: A diagnosis of light-headedness upon standing up.
Inability to move an entire arm is incompatible with neurological pathology.
Loss of sensation in a non-dermatome distribution is anatomically consistent.

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of light-headedness upon standing up.

questions.explanation: The diagnosis of conversion disorder requires the presence of a voluntary motor or sensory symptom; “autonomic” symptoms such as orthostatic light-headedness would not be included in this category and would be better accommodated by a diagnosis of somatic symptom disorder. Tunnel vision (“tubular visual field”) and localized anesthesia for some but not all sensory modalities that are carried in the same nerve distribution are classic examples of sensory deficit symptoms that would be considered functional or psychogenic neurological symptoms. In a patient with a medical/neurological diagnosis such as multiple sclerosis that might account for a new neurological symptom, great caution should be exercised before labeling a symptom as psychogenic or functional, but it is possible even for patients with such illnesses to have functional symptoms.

questions.question_text: How many somatic symptoms are required to meet symptom criteria for the DSM-5 diagnosis of somatic symptom disorder?
questions.explanation: The diagnosis of somatic symptom disorder requires one or more somatic symptoms that are distressing or result in disruption of daily life.

questions.question_text: A girl aged 9 years is brought by her mother with repeated presentations for various medical conditions. The mother appears anxious during visits and frequently requests investigations. Upon further inquiry, the symptoms are inconsistent and clear up when the child is in school without parental observation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Factitious disorder by proxy as when a person feigns or induces illness in a child or others in order to obtain medical attention. A form of child abuse. The pattern of a caregiver producing symptoms that resolve without parental presence is classic for this condition.

questions.question_text: Why is la belle indifférence (apparent lack of concern about the symptom) not included as a diagnostic criterion for conversion disorder (functional neurological symptom disorder)?

options.text: La belle indifférence is now required for conversion disorder diagnosis.
A diagnosis of it has poor specificity.
A diagnosis of it has poor sensitivity.
A diagnosis of it pathologizes stoicism.
La belle indifférence is considered an accurate indicator of psychological origin.

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of it has poor sensitivity.

questions.explanation: Although classically described as a feature of conversion disorder, la belle indifférence (i.e., apparent lack of concern about the nature or implications of the symptom) is not specific for conversion disorder and should not be used to make the diagnosis.

questions.question_text: Somatoform Disorders in DSM-IV are referred to as Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders in DSM-5. which of the following options features characterizes the major diagnosis in this class, somatic symptom disorder?

options.text: A diagnosis of medically unexplained somatic symptoms.
A diagnosis of underlying psychic conflict.
Distressing somatic symptoms and abnormal thoughts, feelings, and behaviors in response to these symptoms.
Somatoform disorders have been completely eliminated from DSM-5.

correct_answer.text: Distressing somatic symptoms and abnormal thoughts, feelings, and behaviors in response to these symptoms.

questions.explanation: Somatic symptom disorder emphasizes diagnosis made on the basis of positive symptoms and signs (distressing somatic symptoms plus abnormal thoughts, feelings, and behaviors in response to these symptoms) rather than the absence of a medical explanation for somatic symptoms. A distinctive characteristic of many individuals with somatic symptom disorder is not the somatic symptoms per se, but instead the way they present and interpret them. Incorporating affective, cognitive, and behavioral components into the criteria for somatic symptom disorder provides a more comprehensive and accurate reflection of the true clinical picture than can be achieved by assessing the somatic complaints alone.

questions.question_text: When a mother knowingly and deceptively reports signs and symptoms of illness in her preschool-aged child, resulting in the child’s hospitalization and subjection to numerous tests and procedures, what diagnosis would be recorded for the child?

options.text: This behavior qualifies as child abuse but not factitious disorder imposed on another.

questions.explanation: Situations in which an individual falsifies illness in another in the absence of obvious external rewards and presents that person to others as ill, impaired, or injured qualify for a diagnosis of factitious disorder imposed on another. This diagnosis pertains to the perpetrator of the falsification, not the Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders victim. In addition to other people, animals (e.g., pets) may be victims of such falsification. The diagnosis of factitious disorder is not made when the behavior is better explained by another mental disorder. The victim of this kind of falsification is not coded as having a mental disorder diagnosis (unless another diagnosis is present). The term Munchausen syndrome is not used in DSM-5, and the DSM-IV term by proxy has been replaced with imposed on another. DSM-5 states that the victim “may” be given an abuse diagnosis (if warranted).

questions.question_text: A disorder characterized by forgetting one's name, personal identity, and episodic memory is:
questions.explanation: Fugue is characterized by forgetting one's name, personal identity, and episodic memory, often involving sudden travel away from home or usual place of work.

questions.question_text: Individuals with dissociative identity disorder are LEAST likely to have which comorbidity?
questions.explanation: Dissociative identity disorder is not associated with schizophrenia but rather with PTSD, depression, personality disorders (especially avoidant and borderline personality disorders), conversion disorder (functional neurological symptom disorder), somatic symptom disorder, eating disorders, substancerelated disorders, obsessive– compulsive disorder, and sleep disorders. questions.question_text: Illness anxiety disorder involves a preoccupation with having or acquiring a serious illness. How severe must the accompanying somatic symptoms be to meet criteria for the diagnosis of illness anxiety disorder?

options.text: A diagnosis of mild to moderate severity.
A diagnosis of moderate to high severity.
A diagnosis of any level of severity.
Mild severity at most, but there need not be any somatic symptoms.
None of the above; the presence of any somatic symptoms rules out the diagnosis of illness anxiety disorder.

correct_answer.text: Mild severity at most, but there need not be any somatic symptoms.

questions.explanation: Criterion B for illness anxiety disorder states, “Somatic symptoms are not present or, if present, are only mild in intensity.” The hallmark of the disorder is chronic, excessive, and disproportionate preoccupation and worry about having or acquiring a serious medical illness, rather than a somatic complaint. If somatic symptoms are present, it is likely that a diagnosis of somatic symptom disorder is more appropriate.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which is a descriptive specifier included in the diagnostic criteria for somatic symptom disorder?

options.text: A diagnosis of with predominant pain.
A diagnosis of with psychological comorbidity.

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of with predominant pain.

questions.explanation: The “with predominant pain” specifier is used for individuals whose somatic symptoms predominantly involve pain.

questions.question_text: Which condition is characterized by exaggerated and catastrophic misinterpretation of body signs and symptoms?
questions.explanation: Hypochondriasis is characterized by exaggerated and catastrophic misinterpretation of body signs and symptoms. This falls under the broader category of disorders of bodily distress or bodily experience.

questions.question_text: The lorazepam challenge test is used in the diagnosis of
questions.explanation: In the ‘lorazepam challenge test’ (coined by George Bidder), an intravenous line is established and a syringe containing 2–4 mg of lorazepam in 2 mL of solution is prepared, and 1 mg is injected. In the next 2–5 minutes if no reduction is observed in catatonic features, the second 1 mg of lorazepam is injected, and the assessment is repeated. It is noted that more than 80% of patients with catatonia have a rapid reduction in symptoms with an intravenous lorazepam challenge. Such a response to lorazepam typically results in a lorazepam treatment trial, followed by electroconvulsive therapy if substantial relief is not maintained. Fink and Taylor suggest that adhering to this algorithm achieves remission of catatonia in almost all patients. Amytal interview using intravenous barbiturates/benzodiazepines has been used in dissociative amnesia/fugue. Bush G, et al. Catatonia, II: treatment with lorazepam and electroconvulsive therapy. Acta Psychiatrica Scandinavica 1996; 93: 137–143. Fink M and Taylor MA. Catatonia: subtype or syndrome in DSM? American Journal of Psychiatry 2006; 163: 1875–1876.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old man is concerned that he looks “weak” and “puny” despite the fact that to neutral observers he appears very muscular. When confronted about his belief he believes he is being humored and that people are in fact making fun of his small size behind his back. He has tried a number of strategies to increase muscle mass, encompassing exercising excessively and using ana bolic steroids; however, he remains dissatisfied with his appearance. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: A diagnosis of delusional disorder, somatic type.
A diagnosis of narcissistic personality disorder.
A diagnosis of body identity integrity disorder.
Body dysmorphic disorder, with muscle dysmorphia.

correct_answer.text: Body dysmorphic disorder, with muscle dysmorphia.

questions.explanation: Muscle dysmorphia is a form of body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) in which an individual—usually a male—is preoccupied with the idea that his body build is too small or insufficiently muscular. Although insight may be so poor as to be considered delusional, the focus on body appearance alone warrants the BDD diagnosis, and the sole focus on perceived appearance differentiates this disorder from personality disorders. Body identity integrity disorder (apotemnophilia) (which is not a DSM-5 disorder) involves a desire to have a limb amputated to correct an experience of mismatch between a person’s sense of body identity and his or her actual anatomy. However, the conObsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders—ANSWER GUIDE | 277 cern does not focus on the limb’s appearance, as it would in BDD. Koro, a culturally related disorder that usually occurs in epidemics in Southeastern Asia, consists of a fear that the penis (labia, nipples, or breasts in females) is shrinking or retracting and will disappear into the abdomen, often accompanied by a belief that death will result. Koro differs from BDD in several ways, including a focus on death rather than preoccupation with perceived ugliness.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which is not a model that has been proposed to explain the relationship between IBS and high rates of psychiatric comorbidity?

options.text: A diagnosis of somatization disorder hypothesis

questions.explanation: Studies of psychiatric comorbidity in IBS estimate rates of comorbidity at 42–64% of all IBS patients. The exact mechanism for high rates of psychiatric comorbidity in IBS is unknown. Four models have been proposed to explain the relationship between IBS and high rates of psychiatric comorbidity. The fi rst model is the somatization disorder hypothesis. This model classifi es IBS as one of a group of diagnoses that can be made from a primary somatization disorder or other somatoform disorder. The somatopsychic hypothesis states that psychological symptoms are the result of chronic gastrointestinal distress and the unsatisfactory interaction with healthcare providers who do not accurately diagnose and treat IBS. Psychogenic hypothesis states that specifi c psychiatric disorders cause IBS for a signifi cant proportion of patients. Panic disorder, in particular, is proposed as a cause for secondary IBS. The self-selection model proposes that psychiatric comorbidity increases the rate of treatment seeking in patients who have IBS. Kaplan HI. Kaplan and Sadock’s Comprehensive Textbook of Psychiatry, 8th edn. Lippincott Williams and Wilkins, 2004 p. 2118.

questions.question_text: A patient presents with a persistent preoccupation with the fear of having a serious undiagnosed disease, with few or no somatic symptoms. All investigations are normal, and the preoccupation persists despite appropriate medical evaluation and reassurance. What is the most likely DSM-5 diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Illness Anxiety Disorder (DSM-5) — previously called hypochondriasis in DSM-IV and ICD-10 — is characterised by persistent preoccupation with the fear of having or acquiring a serious disease, persisting despite appropriate medical evaluation and normal findings, in the absence of significant somatic symptoms (Kaplan & Sadock, p.659; NOTOP, p.1079). The belief is not of delusional intensity (excluding option A) and is not intentionally feigned (excluding option D). Somatic Symptom Disorder (option C) is the preferred DSM-5 diagnosis when prominent somatic symptoms are present alongside disease conviction. Conversion Disorder (option E) involves neurological motor or sensory deficits without organic basis and is not applicable here.

questions.question_text: A 31-year-old man presents with sudden onset of inability to speak (aphonia) after his mother-in-law moved in permanently. Physical examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Sudden onset of neurological symptoms (aphonia) following a psychological stressor with no organic cause suggests dissociative/conversion disorder.

questions.question_text: A patient presents with non-organic limb paralysis. Which test is most useful in confirming functional neurological disorder?
questions.explanation: Hoover's sign (lack of hip extension weakness when the patient flexes the contralateral hip) is a sensitive and specific test for functional limb weakness.

questions.question_text: Patient has visited 5 hospitals at different times and all test done are normal. He is not accepting that everything is normal and convinced that he has cancer
questions.explanation: This presentation describes a delusional disorder with hypochondriacal content, characterized by fixed false beliefs about having a serious disease despite medical reassurance and normal investigations.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which statements is Accurate regarding somatic symptom disorder?

options.text: Good clinical outlook is linked to high socioeconomic status and response to treatment of depression and anxiety symptoms.
Childhoodonset symptoms usually persist into adulthood.
individuals with this disorder must have Inaccurate beliefs that last at least for 1 year.
The presence or absence of la belle indifference is a reliable feature to differentiate from other disorders.

correct_answer.text: Good clinical outlook is linked to high socioeconomic status and response to treatment of depression and anxiety symptoms.

questions.explanation: The above presentation suggests that the patient has somatic symptom disorder. This disorder is characterized by 6 months or more of general and nondelusional preoccupation with bodily symptoms that are misinterpreted by the patient as signs of a severe illness. Typically this preoccupation causes enough distress to impair daily functioning. Patients typically have poor insight concerning this disorder. However, patients with a high socioeconomic status and those who respond to treatment of depression and anxiety typically have a good prognosis throughout the course of the disorder. Re FeRe NCe Sadock, B. J., & Sadock, V. A. (2014). Kaplan and Sadock’s synopsis of psychiatry: Behavioral sciences/ clinical psychiatry (11th ed.). Philadelphia, PA: Lippincott Williams and Wilkins.

questions.question_text: Dissociative amnesia most often involves which of the following types of amnesia?

options.text: A diagnosis of permanent, irreversible amnesia.
Localized or selective amnesia for specific events.
Generalized amnesia is the most common presentation of dissociative amnesia.

correct_answer.text: Localized or selective amnesia for specific events.

questions.explanation: The defining characteristic of dissociative amnesia is an inability to recall important autobiographical information that 1) should be successfully stored in memory and 2) ordinarily would be readily remembered (Criterion A). Dissociative amnesia differs from the permanent amnesias due to neurobiological damage or toxicity that prevent memory storage or retrieval in that it is always potentially reversible because the memory has been successfully stored. Criterion A notes that dissociative amnesia most often consists of localized or selective amnesia for a specific event or events; or generalized amnesia for identity and life history. Localized amnesia, a failure to recall events during a circumscribed period of time, is the most common form of dissociative amnesia. In selective amnesia, the individual can recall some, but not all, of the events during a circumscribed period of time. Thus, the individual may remember part of a traumatic event but not other parts. Some individuals report both localized and selective amnesias. Generalized amnesia, a complete loss of memory for one’s life history, is rare. Individuals with generalized amnesia may forget personal identity. Some lose previous knowledge about the world (i.e., semantic knowledge) and can no longer access well-learned skills (i.e., procedural knowledge). Generalized amnesia may be more common among combat veterans, sexual assault victims, and individuals experiencing extreme emotional stress or conflict. Individuals with dissociative amnesia are frequently unaware (or only partially aware) of their memory problems. Many, especially those with localized amnesia, minimize the importance of their memory loss and may become uncomfortable when prompted to address it. In systematized amnesia, the individual loses memory for a specific category of information (e.g., all memories relating to one’s family, a particular person, or childhood sexual abuse). In continuous amnesia, an individual forgets each new event as it occurs.

questions.question_text: A patient presents with paralysis of his arm after his friend died in a motorcycle accident, but neurological examination and imaging reveal no structural abnormality. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Conversion disorder involves loss of motor or sensory function without identifiable neurological cause, typically following significant psychic stress or trauma, as in this case.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old woman is hospitalized for evaluation of episodes in which she appears to lose consciousness, rocks her head from side to side, and moves her arms and legs in a nonsynchronous, bicycling pattern. The episodes occur a few times per day and last for 2–5 minutes. Electroencephalography during the episodes does not reveal any ictal activity. Immediately after a fit, her sensorium appears clear. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: A diagnosis of somatic symptom disorder.
Conversion disorder (functional neurological symptom disorder), with attacks or seizures.

correct_answer.text: Conversion disorder (functional neurological symptom disorder), with attacks or seizures.

questions.explanation: The essential feature of conversion disorder (functional neurological symptom disorder) is the presence of one or more symptoms that cause clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning (or warrant medical attention); are incompatible with recognized neurological or medical conditions; and cannot be better exSomatic Symptom and Related Disorders—ANSWER GUIDE | 315 plained by another mental disorder. This patient’s pattern of movement, duration of attack, and return to clear consciousness at the end of the attack are incompatible with a diagnosis of epilepsy (as is underscored by the electroencephalogram) and lack resemblance to any other medical or neurological disorder that would account for them. Although factitious disorder, with conscious feigning of symptoms, has not been absolutely ruled out, the diagnosis of conversion disorder does not require certainty that symptoms are not consciously feigned, in recognition of the fact that reliability in ascertaining conscious feigning is poor. Positive evidence of feigning would rule out conversion disorder; in that case, the diagnosis would be factitious disorder.

questions.question_text: A man whose friend died in a motorcycle accident now presents with a paralyzed arm despite doctors finding no neurological issues. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This presentation is characteristic of dissociative neurological symptom disorder (formerly called conversion disorder in DSM-IV), characterized by motor symptoms that imply involuntary discontinuity in normal function and are not consistent with recognized neurological disease.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which is accurate about adjustment disorders?

options.text: They are diagnosed twice as often in women than in men.
In children and adolescents, boys are diagnosed as commonly as girls.
They are one of the most common psychiatric diagnoses in medically hospitalized individuals.
Single women are affected more commonly than married women.

questions.explanation: The prevalence of the disorder is from 2% to 8% of the general population. Women are diagnosed with the disorder twice as often as men. Single women are overrepresented in this patient population. In children and adolescents, boys and girls are equally diagnosed. Adjustment disorders are one of the most common psychiatric diagnoses in hospitalized patients for medical and surgical problems. The percentage of individuals in outpatient mental health treatment with a principal diagnosis of an adjustment disorder ranges between 5% and 20%. In a hospital psychiatric consultation setting, adjustment disorder is one of the most common diagnoses, with a prevalence rate of almost 50%.

questions.question_text: A 50-year-old man with hard-to-control hypertension acknowledges to his physician that he regularly “takes breaks” from his medication regimen because he was brought up with the belief that pills are bad and natural remedies are better. He is well aware that his blood pressure becomes dangerously high when he does not follow the regimen. Which diagnosis most accurately describes this case?

options.text: A diagnosis of nonadherence to medical treatment.
A diagnosis of unspecified anxiety disorder.
A diagnosis of denial of medical illness.
Psychological factors affecting other medical conditions.

correct_answer.text: Psychological factors affecting other medical conditions.

questions.explanation: DSM-5 includes nonadherence to medical treatment as a matter that may be the subject of clinical attention but not as a diagnosis per se. It receives a V code. If noncompliance becomes the major focus of clinical attention, then the V code would apply. We do not have evidence to support a diagnosis of an anxiety disorder. Denial of illness is not a diagnosis, although it may certainly command clinical attention, and the use of denial as a coping mechanism, if it interferes with obtaining treatment in a timely way, would be an example of a psychological factor affecting another medical condition; however, this patient does not deny his hypertension or the potential consequences. An adjustment disorder diagnosis applies to a clinically significant psychological response to a stressor, such as mood or anxiety symptoms. The diagnosis of psychological factors affecting another medical condition applies when a medical symptom or condition is present AND psychological or behavioral factors adversely affect the medical condition in one of the following ways: 1) close temporal association of the psychological factor and the onset or exacerbation or delay in recovery of the medical condition; 2) the factors interfere with treatment; 3) the factors add to the individual’s health risk; 4) the factors influence the pathophysiology to precipitate or exacerbate symptoms. In this vignette, the patient’s long-standing belief that pills are “bad” interferes with treatment adherence for his acknowledged hypertension, adding to his health risk.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which is considered a “positive” dissociative symptom?
questions.explanation: Dissociative symptoms can affect all psychological functions and are usually divided into positive and negative symptoms. Positive symptoms include intrusions into

questions.question_text: A man who witnessed a friend's death 6 weeks ago is unable to move a limb despite absence of neurological deficit. This presentation is most consistent with:
questions.explanation: The presentation of neurological symptoms (limb paralysis) without corresponding neurological pathology following a psychological stressor is characteristic of conversion disorder, now termed Dissociative Neurological Symptom Disorder in ICD-11.

questions.question_text: A woman presents with multiple gynaecological and gastrointestinal complaints over 10 years with all tests normal. She remains convinced doctors have missed something. Which diagnosis best fits?
questions.explanation: Somatic symptom disorder involves multiple physical symptoms across different body systems with excessive health concern and normal investigations over an extended period.

questions.question_text: Hypochondriasis is characterized by which of the following?

options.text: Abnormal preoccupation with health and fear of disease despite physical evidence to the contrary
Primary belief that symptoms are psychological
Significant functional impairment exclusively from physical symptoms

correct_answer.text: Abnormal preoccupation with health and fear of disease despite physical evidence to the contrary

questions.explanation: Hypochondriasis involves abnormal preoccupation with one's health and a fear of having or acquiring a disease despite physical evidence to the contrary, now classified under OCD and related disorders in ICD-11.

questions.question_text: Which of the following treatment approaches has been the best evident to support dissociative fugue?

options.text: Psychodynamic treatment to integrate the identity that participated in fugue

correct_answer.text: Psychodynamic treatment to integrate the identity that participated in fugue

questions.explanation: Dissociative fugue is treated primarily with an eclectic, psychodynamically oriented psychotherapy that focuses on helping the patient recover memory for identity and recent experience (Kaplan & Sadock, p.1003). Hypnotherapy and pharmacologically facilitated interviews are also used as adjunctive techniques to assist with memory recovery. Group treatment with peers (option C) has no established evidence base as a treatment for dissociative fugue.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which is considered a POOR prognostic symptom in conversion disorder (functional neurological symptom disorder)?

options.text: A diagnosis of comorbid medical illness

questions.explanation: The following are poor prognostic symptoms in conversion disorder: pseudoseizure (psychogenic nonepileptic seizure), psychogenic tremor, subclinical (undiagnosed) personality pathology, concomitant medical illness, the presence of a stuffed animal brought to the hospital by the patient, poor perception of own wellbeing, motor symptoms, and pending litigation. Re FeRe NCe Allin, M., Streeruwitz, A., & Curtis, V. (2005). Progress in understanding conversion disorder. Neuropsychiatric Disease and Treatment, 1, 205– 209.

questions.question_text: A man whose friend died in a motorcycle accident now presents with a paralyzed arm despite comprehensive neurological investigations finding no organic pathology. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Dissociative neurological symptom disorder (formerly conversion disorder in DSM-5) is characterized by motor, sensory, or cognitive symptoms that imply an involuntary discontinuity in normal integration of these functions and are not consistent with recognized disease of the nervous system. The symptoms are not due to substance effects or other medical conditions.

questions.question_text: Patients with conversion disorder as opposed to malingering are more likely to display which of the following symptoms?

options.text: Provide extremely detailed description of events leading to their illness

questions.explanation: Those with conversion disorder are often dependent, clingy, friendly, and cooperative, compared to those with malingering who are suspicious and aloof.

questions.question_text: Which dissociative disorder involves inability to recall traumatic experiences?
questions.explanation: Dissociative amnesia is characterized by inability to remember traumatic experiences, distinguishing it from other dissociative presentations.

questions.question_text: A 20-year-old man exhibits the complaint of acute onset of decreased visual acuity in his left eye. Physical, neurological, and laboratory examinations are entirely normal, encompassing stereopsis testing, fogging test, and brain magnetic resonance imaging. The remainder of the history is negative except for the patient’s report that since his midteens he has felt that his left cheekbone and eyebrow are too big. He spends a lot of time comparing the right and left sides of his face in the mirror. He is planning to have plastic surgery as soon as he graduates from college. which of the following options diagnoses are suggested?

options.text: Tunnel vision with a fixed diameter at all distances suggests organic vision loss.
The finding of tunnel vision is incompatible with conversion disorder.
Body dysmorphic disorder and conversion disorder (functional neurological symptom disorder).
Preserved pupillary reflexes are diagnostic of true neurological blindness.
A diagnosis of delusional disorder, somatic subtype.

correct_answer.text: Body dysmorphic disorder and conversion disorder (functional neurological symptom disorder).

questions.explanation: The vision complaint and normal examinations are consistent with a diagnosis of a functional neurological symptom disorder, specifically a functional visual acuity problem (“special sensory” subtype of conversion disorder). The long-standing concern about the appearance of the left side of his face is consistent with a diagnosis of body dysmorphic disorder, as is the plan for plastic surgery in the absence of any visible cosmetic defect. An individual can have both of these diagnoses. One might speculate about the relationship, in this case, of preoccupation with the appearance of the left side of the face in particular and the development of functional symptoms in the left eye, but these speculations are beyond the scope of DSM-5 diagnosis. Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders—ANSWER GUIDE | 317

questions.question_text: A woman is unable to remember her personal identity. Which dissociative disorder best describes her presentation?
questions.explanation: Dissociative identity disorder is characterized by the presence of two or more distinct personality states and fragmented identity, including inability to remember personal identity and important personal information.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which is not a feature of chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS)?

options.text: Fatigue worsened by minimal physical exertion

questions.explanation: The Center for Disease Control defi nition of CFS (also called neurasthenia and myalgic encephalitis in the UK) consists of severe unexplained fatigue for over 6 months. This is of new or defi nite onset; not due to continuing exertion; not resolved by rest; and is functionally impairing. The criterion also mentions other symptoms that are suggestive of CFS, out of which at least four need to be present for the diagnosis. They are impaired memory or concentration; sore throat; tender lymph nodes; muscle pain; pain in several joints; new pattern of headaches; unrefreshing sleep; postexertional malaise lasting more than 24 hours. Although non-refreshing sleep is a criterion, late insomnia is not. Gelder M, Harrison P, and Cowen P. Shorter Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry, 5th edn. Oxford University Press, 2006, p. 387.

questions.question_text: Which pattern of body concern is most often associated with body dysmorphic disorder?

options.text: Concern about multiple different areas of the body
Emphasis on the thighs and stomach
Intense preoccupation with weight and shape concerns
Possessing good insight about their actual versus desired appearance

correct_answer.text: Concern about multiple different areas of the body

questions.explanation: The most common concern in patients with body dysmorphic disorder involves the face and head and can also include the skin, nose, and hair. Most patients with body dysmorphic disorder worry about five to seven different body areas.

questions.question_text: A 32-year-old woman exhibits concerns regarding her ‘ugly appearance’. She had been convinced for a long time that her appearance was defective and was particularly worried about her ‘streak’ eyes. She admitted spending at least 14–16 hours a day thinking about her appearance and comparing herself with other people or seeking reassurance from others. Which of the following is true with regard to the treatment of this condition?

options.text: She may respond to higher than usual antidepressant doses of serotonin re-uptake inhibitors (SSRIs)
There is a good evidence for response to psychotherapy alone in this condition
She has a comparable likelihood of response to SSRIs and non-SSRID antidepressants
She will require a longer than usual duration of treatment trial with SSRIs
Cognitive behavioural treatment (CBT) has no role in the treatment

correct_answer.text: She may respond to higher than usual antidepressant doses of serotonin re-uptake inhibitors (SSRIs)

questions.explanation: The amount of evidence for treatment of body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) is limited, but it is accepted that serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and cognitive–behavioural therapy (CBT) are the treatments of choice. Antidepressants, antipsychotics, or electroconvulsive therapy are not effi cacious for BDD, even though the data are limited. BDD symptoms of delusional patients appear as likely as symptoms of non-delusional patients to respond to an SSRI. SSRIs improve preoccupations, distress, and insight with an associated reduction in BDD-related behaviours such as mirror-checking, etc. The patient need not have depression to experience the benefi cial effect. Although data are limited with respect to dose-fi nding studies, it is accepted that BDD often requires higher SSRI doses than those typically used in the treatment of depression, with variable response times ranging from 4–5 weeks to 9 weeks. Many patients may thus require longer than the usual treatment trial. Phillips KA. Pharmacologic treatment of body dysmorphic disorder: review of the evidence and a recommended treatment approach. CNS Spectrums 2002; 7: 453–60.

individuals with the disorder disproportionately work in the healthcare field.
